name: Calf implants

card.summary: Silicone implants placed in the lower leg to add calf volume; documented in surgical case series with notable complications such as compartment syndrome.
card.note: Evidence is surgeon-reported case series and literature reviews, not controlled trials; rare but serious complications such as compartment syndrome are reported.

quick.overview:
Calf implants are silicone prostheses placed under the fascia or muscle of the lower leg to increase calf size or correct asymmetry or wasting. Published use includes aesthetic cases, bodybuilders and reconstruction after injury or illness.

The literature is mostly case series and reviews from individual surgeons. Fat grafting is the main alternative technique described.
quick.mechanism: A surgeon makes an incision, typically behind the knee, and places a solid or gel-filled silicone implant either beneath the fascia or in a plane between the calf muscles. Fat grafting and combined 'composite' approaches are also described.
quick.risks: A review of 26 studies analysed complication rates by technique. Reported problems include seroma, implant displacement, capsular contracture, dissatisfaction leading to removal and, in one case, acute compartment syndrome with muscle necrosis. Regulation of implants and surgeons varies by country.

lead: Calf augmentation is a cosmetic and reconstructive surgery that adds volume to the lower leg, most often with silicone implants placed beneath the fascia or muscle, and sometimes with fat grafting. [1][2] Indications include thin legs, asymmetry, bodybuilders seeking more muscle size and deformity from injury or illness. [1][2]

How it improves looks is direct and structural: the implant adds volume and projection where muscle is thin, so the lower leg looks fuller from the front and side, and legs in shorts or a swimsuit look more proportionate to the thighs. Surgeons describe it for thin legs, asymmetry and post-injury or post-illness defects as well as for bodybuilders [1].

Calf implants were first reported in 1979, and early designs included silicone-gel implants and firm silicone rubber ones, with placement below the deep fascia and, later, in the plane between gastrocnemius and soleus. [3] Surgeons have published single-center series and a 2019 review pooling 26 studies on 1,498 patients and 2,629 calves. [2]

Available evidence is limited to such series and reviews; no randomized trials were found. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities the procedure is a niche topic, usually raised by people whose calves stay small despite training.

paras: Implants are made of solid semisoft silicone, which can be carved to fit, or of a firm shell containing cohesive silicone. [4] A 2000 report favoured soft silicone implants as more natural-looking than hard ones, placed over the gastrocnemius or beneath the fascia through an incision at the popliteal crease. [5]

A submuscular approach, between the gastrocnemius and soleus, was developed because subfascial implants had visible capsular contracture problems and firm implants could be felt through the skin. [3] A 2009 anthropometric study classified calf defects into five types to guide implant type, size and plane. [6] Fat grafting for calf augmentation has been reported as an alternative to silicone implants, and combined composite augmentation in staged procedures has been described. [7][8]

A 2009 anthropometric study looked at 2,600 photographs of standing women and took calf measurements in 168 women aged 15 to 61, to define the features that make calves look attractive and to catalogue defects into five types that guide implant selection [6]. A 25-year experience paper pairs surgical results with an anatomical review of the region [10]. Surgeons also describe operating on under-developed calves after treatment of congenital clubfoot deformity, a reconstructive use [11].

The surgical literature describes three broad groups of patients. Aesthetic patients have naturally slim or underdeveloped lower legs. Reconstructive patients have a deformity after injury, illness or a congenital condition. A third group is made up of bodybuilders and other athletes whose calves remain small relative to the rest of the physique. [1] In the 1991 to 2016 series, 23 of 50 patients were treated for aesthetic reasons, six were bodybuilders and 21 had lower-leg reconstruction after illness-related deformity, an unusually high proportion of reconstructive cases for a calf series. [1]

Series differ in who they treat. A Stockholm series of 18 patients had 13 women and five men, while a 2000 series of 100 patients had 95 women and five men. [4][5] The authors of a 2019 review of 26 studies note that attention to calf appearance has been growing in both men and women, and they analysed demographics, including age and gender, alongside complication rates. [2]

Surgeons also describe calf appearance in terms of proportion. The 2009 anthropometric study measured the legs of 168 women aged 15 to 61 to identify front-to-back and side-to-side projection ratios that consistently make legs look attractive, and it sorted calf defects into five types that guide the choice of implant design, size and plane. [6] Implants can also be used for asymmetry, where one calf is smaller than the other. [5]

The first implants were placed below the deep fascia of the calf, and later surgeons described moving the implant into the plane between the gastrocnemius and soleus muscles to hide the edges of firm implants and reduce capsular problems. [3] The senior author of the 2017 series reports introducing technical modifications over a 25-year experience, including a purpose-designed inserter instrument for placing calf implants. [1][10]

Fat grafting is described as an autologous alternative that avoids a foreign implant and lets the surgeon shape the medial and lateral calf separately. [7] Composite augmentation combines an implant with fat grafting in a staged procedure, and its authors stress anatomical features and health conditions that affect safety. [8] Surgeons have also applied calf augmentation to under-developed calves left after treatment of congenital clubfoot. [11]

No randomized trials were identified. Evidence consists of case series and reviews. A 2017 series covering 1991-2016 included 50 patients who had 60 calf corrections, 23 aesthetic and 21 reconstructive; the surgeon rated results excellent-to-good in 30 of 37 followed patients and patients rated results very good in 18, good in 10, acceptable in 7 and bad in 2. [1]

A 2000 series of 100 patients (200 implants) reported no infections, ruptures or hematomas, four seromas that resolved, and removal of four implants in two dissatisfied patients. [5] A 2005 report described 18 patients at a Stockholm clinic, and a 2017 study examined the safety and efficacy of subfascial augmentation. [4][9]
A 2019 review analysed complication rates for subfascial implants, submuscular implants and fat grafting across 26 studies from 1993 to 2018. [2]

The 2000 series operated on 100 patients (95 women and 5 men) between 1985 and 1999, using mainly soft Glitzenstein implants, and its author reported that patients walked about eight hours after surgery and that no functional problem or muscular dysfunction had been seen [5]. A report on fat grafting for calf augmentation and reshaping presents an autologous alternative to silicone [7].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities
paras: Calf implants appear in forum talk mostly as a half-serious fallback for genetically small calves. On T Nation a member writes that they would "totally get calf implants" once they are big but still stuck with small calves [12]. Other posts mention implants in passing, including a poster who recalls a television programme about a man who had calf, pectoral and gluteal implants, and a remark that a female bodybuilder obtained calf implants to match large thighs [13][14].
These are anecdotes rather than data. The surgical literature describes bodybuilders among the patients who seek the procedure [1].

In the 2017 series, one 28-year-old professional bodybuilder developed acute anterior compartment syndrome in one leg; the implants were removed after 16 hours but muscle ischaemia and necrosis followed, requiring several operations. [1] Other reported issues include seroma, implant displacement and capsular contracture. [5][3] Anatomical and physiological considerations, including some health conditions, are cited as relevant to safety in staged composite augmentation. [8]

timeline.event: First report of calf augmentation, per a later surgical review. [3]
Technique of placing implants under the investing crural fascia worked out. [1]
Submuscular placement between gastrocnemius and soleus reported in six patients. [3]
Series covering 1991 to 2016 reports long-term results including a compartment syndrome case in a bodybuilder. [1]
Literature review of 26 studies and 1,498 patients analyses complications by technique. [2]

lore.intro: Calf implants come up on bodybuilding forums as an option for people whose calves resist growth, mentioned in passing rather than as a developed topic [12][13].

claims.claim: Calf implants can fix calves that will not grow with training
claims.believers: A forum member says they would get calf implants once big, despite small calves [12].
claims.experts: Surgical series report that implants add volume and that surgeons rate most results good to excellent, with complications that include seroma, displacement and, rarely, compartment syndrome [1][5].

claims.believers: Forum comments about implants in bodybuilding are often sceptical or joking [13][14].
claims.experts: One 2017 series describes acute compartment syndrome with muscle necrosis in a professional bodybuilder, and a 2019 review compared complication rates across techniques [1][2].

chain: Silicone implant placed under the fascia or between the calf muscles
Adds volume and projection to the lower leg
angle.text: A silicone implant adds permanent bulk behind the lower leg without relying on muscle growth. Surgeons also use it to correct asymmetry or wasting after injury or illness.
